name: Magudeswarar Temple, Kodumudi
deity: Shiva as Magudeswarar (Kodumudinathar), with the goddess Vadivudai Nayaki (Soundaranayaki)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine on the Kaveri, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); inscriptions of the Pandya, Kongu Chola and Vijayanagara eras
dynasty: Pandya patronage, with Kongu Chola, Kongu Pandya and Vijayanagara-era records
summary: Magudeswarar is the Shiva temple on the Kaveri's bank at Kodumudi, the Tiruppandikodumudi of the Tevaram, praised by the three great Tevaram saints and remembered as a rare precinct where Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma are all worshipped.

sections.history: Kodumudi lies on the Kaveri in the Kongu country, and its temple is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, praised in the hymns of Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar, the three great saints of the Tevaram. Tradition ties the place to the Pandya kings, whose patronage is remembered in the older name Tiruppandikodumudi. Inscriptions at the temple and on the river bank span several centuries, with records attributed to a 12th-century Kerala chieftain, the Kongu Cholas of the 13th century, Kongu Pandya rulers in 1288 and 1291 CE, and Vijayanagara-period donors, largely gifts for lamps and offerings. Devotional literature claims far greater antiquity, which cannot be confirmed here; what is certain is a long, unbroken life of worship. It is reckoned the sixth of the Kongu temples sung in the Tevaram.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east and spreads across a large rectangular enclosure, said to measure some 640 by 484 feet, with tradition crediting a Pandya king with raising three gopurams. Beside the sanctum of Magudeswarar, also called Kodumudinathar, and the shrine of the goddess, stand a shrine of Vishnu as Veeranarayana Perumal and a shrine of Brahma. This is why the place is called a Trimurti temple, a rare precinct where the three gods share a single roof of worship. The sacred tree of the temple is the vanni, beneath which devotees place stone images of the serpent. The temple rises on the bank of the Kaveri, with a rock standing in the river just opposite.
sections.legends: Tradition links Kodumudi to the sage Agastya. A rock in the Kaveri opposite the temple is said to be where a crow overturned the sage's water pot, and another tale says he caught the lingam in his hand as it seemed to vanish, leaving his finger marks upon it. A further story tells of a contest between Vayu, the wind, and Adisesha, the serpent, who coiled around Mount Meru; when peaks were shattered, a gem fell here and became the self-manifested lingam. From the serpent's crown, the magudam, the Lord is remembered as Magudeswarar, and the temple is sought by devotees for relief from afflictions of the serpent planets. Brahma is shown here with three faces, the vanni tree being spoken of as his fourth.
sections.festivals: The great festival is the eleven-day Chithirai Thiruvizha in April and May, when the deities are carried out in procession. Aadi Perukku, in July and August, draws large crowds to the Kaveri bank to honour the river. Arudra Darisanam in the month of Margazhi (December to January) is also observed with devotion, and special worship marks new-moon, full-moon and Pradosham days. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Come first to the Kaveri and look across the water to the rock standing in the stream, then enter the temple at an unhurried pace. Pay homage to Magudeswarar and to the goddess Vadivudai Nayaki, and then walk to the shrines of Vishnu and Brahma, for it is uncommon to find all three gods honoured within one wall. Sit for a while near the vanni tree, where devotees place their serpent stones and make quiet vows. The town is small and the river wide, and the temple keeps the calm of a place long loved by pilgrims.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening (some listings give roughly 6 am to noon and 4 pm to 9 pm); confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Kodumudi lies on the Tiruchirappalli–Karur–Kodumudi–Erode road, about 40 km from Erode and some 25 km from Karur. Kodumudi railway station, on the Erode–Tiruchirappalli line, is about 2 km from the temple. Buses serve the town from Erode, Karur and Coimbatore, and Coimbatore, with the region's airport, is around 100 km away.
